cues.text: MIT 8107, Software Development Lifecycle.
Study Session 5: CI/CD, DevOps and Release Management.
Chapter 1: DevOps and continuous delivery.
Let us begin with the big idea.
DevOps integrates development and operations through shared responsibility, automation, collaboration, feedback and continuous improvement.
Historically, the people who wrote software and the people who ran it in production were often separate teams with separate goals.
DevOps brings them together.
Both sides share responsibility for the software, from the first line of code to its life in production.
They automate repetitive work, they collaborate closely, they gather feedback from real operation, and they keep improving.
To remember what DevOps stands on, the source gives us a framework called CALMS.
That is C, A, L, M, S.
C is Culture.
A is Automation.
L is Lean.
M is Measurement.
And S is Sharing.
So CALMS summarises Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing.
Next, DevSecOps.
DevSecOps embeds security in every stage, rather than treating it as a final gate.
Picture the old habit of building everything and only then asking security to check it at the very end.
DevSecOps rejects that.
Security is present at every stage of the lifecycle.
Now three terms that are often confused, so let us separate them carefully.
First, CI, continuous integration.
CI means integrating changes frequently into a shared repository, with automated build and test feedback.
So developers merge often, and every merge triggers an automated build and tests that tell them quickly whether something broke.
Second, continuous delivery.
Continuous delivery keeps every qualified change releasable, with a production approval or decision where required.
So the change has passed its checks and could go live, but a person or a decision process may still choose whether and when to release it.
Third, continuous deployment.
Continuous deployment automatically deploys qualified changes to production.
The difference from continuous delivery is exactly that final step: in continuous deployment, there is no manual approval; qualified changes go straight to production automatically.
And one more warning from the source: CI/CD is not the same as DevOps culture.
A pipeline is a technical mechanism.
DevOps culture is about shared responsibility, collaboration and improvement.
Having one does not mean you have the other.
Now let us look at the pipeline itself.
The source gives a text diagram, and I will walk you through it in order.
Please look at the accompanying visual, since the arrows show the flow.
It begins with a commit or pull request, written commit slash PR.
That flows to lint, which is automated checking of code style and obvious problems.
Then unit tests.
Then security and dependency checks.
The diagram continues on the next line: build an immutable artifact.
Immutable means it is not changed after it is built.
Then integration and staging tests.
Then, approval if delivery, meaning that where the organisation practises continuous delivery, a human approval step sits here.
Then progressive deploy, meaning the release is rolled out gradually rather than all at once.
Then monitor.
And finally, rollback or roll forward if needed: if something goes wrong, you either return to the previous version, or you move forward with a fix.
Now the practices that make such a pipeline work well.
Build once, and promote the same artifact to each environment.
You do not rebuild for staging and again for production; the exact thing that was tested is the thing that is released.
Environment-specific configuration and secrets are kept separate from code.
Then a series of habits.
Fail fast, so problems surface as early as possible.
Parallelise suitable checks, running them side by side to save time.
Isolate tests so they do not interfere with one another.
Pin dependencies, fixing exact versions.
And protect branches and artifacts from unauthorised or accidental change.
Use caching for repeatable inputs, not unverified binaries.
Caching speeds things up, but only inputs that can be reproduced belong in a cache, not binaries nobody has verified.
Automate regression and policy gates.
And where these produce false positives, meaning warnings that are not real problems, there should be reviewed exception processes, so exceptions are deliberate and checked, not casually ignored.
Then a sharp caution: a fast pipeline with poor tests amplifies failures.
Speed is only valuable if the tests are good.
Otherwise you simply ship defects faster.
Finally, the tools.
Jenkins, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI automate workflows.
Docker packages the application and its runtime in images.
Kubernetes orchestrates containers.
Terraform and Ansible support Infrastructure as Code, abbreviated IaC, and configuration.
Prometheus and Grafana provide metrics and visualisation: Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for visualising them.
But remember: tools are means, not a guarantee of DevOps.
Owning the tools does not make a team DevOps.
On Infrastructure as Code: it should be versioned, reviewed, tested and protected, and teams should detect drift, which is when the real environment departs from what the code describes.
Secrets belong in managed secret stores or CI secrets, with scoped credentials, meaning credentials limited to only what they need.
And supply-chain protection includes dependency pinning, an SBOM, which stands for software bill of materials, signed and verified artifacts, limited build privileges, and vulnerability assessment.
